enExplain: A roadside phone on motorways for contacting emergency services if you break down.
A free phone fixed beside the motorway that links you to help and shows your location.
Police, fire, and ambulance teams called to help at serious incidents.
Braking as quickly and safely as possible to avoid a collision.
A free roadside phone on motorways that connects you to operators who can send help.
Coming out from a junction or side road onto another road.
A sign meaning earlier parking or waiting limits no longer apply beyond that point.
Slowing the vehicle by changing to a lower gear so the engine helps reduce speed.
How fast the engine is turning; often shown on the rev counter (tachometer).
Causing less harm to the environment, e.g. lower emissions.
Electronic Stability Control: a system that helps keep the car stable if wheels start to lose grip.
A car with an extended rear area for carrying more luggage.
Permanently marking the vehicle’s number plate onto glass or parts.
Gases and particles released from a vehicle’s exhaust into the air.
The pipes and parts that carry waste gases from the engine out of the vehicle.
Door mirrors on longer arms so you can still see past a wide trailer or caravan.
Extra or extended side mirrors required when a trailer is wider than the towing vehicle.
Countryside used for farming, where animals or slow farm vehicles may be near the road.
Extreme tiredness that reduces concentration and safe driving ability.
The cover that seals the fuel tank opening after refuelling.
When motorcyclists or cyclists move carefully between lanes or past slow queues of traffic.
Immediate care given to an injured person before professional help arrives.
A set of basic medical supplies for treating minor injuries at the scene.
People trained to give basic emergency care before professionals arrive.
Briefly switch the headlights on and off to get someone's attention.
Briefly switch headlights on and off only to let others know you are there—not to claim priority.
Briefly switching headlights on and off to attract attention; not a reliable way to give instructions.
Briefly switches headlights on and off—often to ask for room to pass, not to demand you speed up.
An amber traffic light that blinks on and off at a pelican crossing.
Orange warning lights that flash to alert drivers, often near schools when children may be about.
Water covering part of the road after heavy rain or flooding, which can wet the brakes.
Deep water covering the road after heavy rain or flooding.
Skin that looks unusually red or warm, for example from heat or emotion.
Extra lights for very poor visibility in fog; use only when conditions are bad enough.
The gap you leave between your vehicle and the one in front.
Driving with too little space behind another vehicle (tailgating), which is unsafe.
The main brake pedal operated with your foot to slow or stop the vehicle.
Paths for people walking, usually beside a road (pavements/sidewalks).
A system that sends power to all four wheels to improve grip, especially on slippery or uneven surfaces.
Extra front lights used only when visibility is seriously reduced, such as in thick fog.
Extra front lights used only when visibility is seriously reduced, such as in thick fog.
How much fuel the vehicle uses; higher use means more cost and emissions.
Driving in a way that uses less fuel, often by smoother acceleration and steadier speed.
Headlights on their brightest, longest setting; can dazzle others, so not for use in fog or when meeting traffic.
Headlights aimed high for maximum range; can dazzle oncoming drivers.
Headlights on their brightest setting; can dazzle others if used wrongly.
Headlights on their brightest, longest setting; must be dipped so you do not dazzle other drivers.
The part of the car that contains the gears for changing speed and power.
Let other traffic go first when they have priority, instead of continuing ahead of them.
Let other traffic go first when they have priority, instead of continuing ahead of them.
Road markings at a junction where you must let other traffic go first.
Vehicles built mainly to carry cargo rather than passengers.
A sat-nav system that gives turn-by-turn directions while you drive.
A flashing green warning light used by certain medical vehicles responding to emergencies.
Optional green ‘P’ plates some new drivers display to show they are newly qualified.
A mobile phone that you hold in your hand while using it.
The vehicle’s owner manual with operating and safety information.
The parking brake, normally used to hold the vehicle when stopped, not for slowing in motion.
The parking brake that holds the vehicle still when stopped.
How the car steers, corners, and responds; a heavy load can make this worse.
A phone you can use without holding it, for example with a speaker or Bluetooth kit.
The emergency lane at the side of a motorway, normally for stopping only in an emergency.
Braking suddenly and hard instead of smoothly and early.
A painted zone with diagonal stripes that separates traffic streams.
Anything on or near the road that could cause danger or force you to change speed or direction.
All indicators flashing together to warn others of a hazard or breakdown.
All indicators flashing together to warn others of danger or a problem.
Warning symbols or plates that show a load’s danger type.
Both indicators flashing together to warn other drivers of a hazard or sudden slowing.
A triangular road sign that warns of a danger or difficult situation ahead on the road.
Dangerous substances such as chemicals or fuel that need special care in transport.
Short for hazard warning lights: all indicators flashing to warn of danger or a stop.
The padded support behind your head on the seat, often called a headrest.
A lot of blood loss from a wound that needs urgent pressure and help.
Large trucks that carry freight; often called HGVs in the UK.
Water thrown up by tyres on a wet road, which can reduce visibility.
Moving livestock (such as sheep or cattle) along or across a road.
High-visibility clothing (bright/reflective) that makes a person easier to see, especially in poor light.
A higher gear used for faster cruising, with less engine braking effect than a low gear.
The main shopping street in a town or city centre.
A tall vehicle such as a lorry or van that can be strongly affected by side winds.
Tall vehicles such as lorries or vans that can be pushed sideways by strong wind.
The official UK rules and advice for road users.
The top of a hill where your view of the road ahead is often limited.
Moving off from a standstill on an uphill slope without rolling back.
A person riding a horse on or beside the road; treat them as vulnerable road users.
People riding horses on or beside the road.
A bridge with a sharp rise in the middle that can hide traffic beyond it.
An accident, breakdown, or other unexpected event on the road.
Using your direction indicators to show you intend to turn or change lane.
Flashing lights on a vehicle used to show you intend to turn or change lane.
A policy that can cover costs after an accident, damage, or claim.
A document that proves your vehicle has valid insurance cover.
The rear-view mirror inside the car, usually at the top of the windscreen.
A small wheel near the trailer hitch used to support and manoeuvre the trailer when unhitched.
A place where roads meet or cross, such as a T-junction or crossroads.
A side road joining the main road on a curve, which can reduce visibility.
Places where roads meet or cross; smaller road users can be harder to spot there.
The raised stone or concrete edge between the road and the pavement (US: curb).
The raised stone or concrete edge between the road and the pavement.
Pressing the accelerator hard in an automatic car so it changes to a lower gear for quicker acceleration.
When one or more lanes are temporarily closed, often due to roadworks or an incident.
Painted lines on the road that show where each traffic lane is.
A seat belt that goes only across the hips, without a diagonal shoulder strap.
Big trucks that carry freight; often called LGVs in the UK.
Older petrol that contained lead; not used for normal road cars today.
Someone learning to drive, often showing L plates on the vehicle.
In the UK, the lane nearest the left-hand side of the road (kerb side) for normal driving.
A place where a road crosses a railway line, often with barriers and warning lights.
A place where a road crosses a railway line, often with barriers and warning lights.
The official body that issues and manages driving licences (in Great Britain, the DVLA).
The official body that issues and manages driving licences and related vehicle records (e.g. DVLA).
The official body that issues and manages driving licences (Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency).
When you cannot see far enough ahead because something blocks your view.
A lane that is open for normal moving traffic (not closed or for emergency use only).
Farm animals such as sheep or cattle that may be on or near the road.
A council tip or recycling centre that accepts items like used engine oil.
A temporary alternative path around a closed or blocked road.
A very lengthy type of road vehicle, such as a lorry, coach, or articulated truck.
Small loose stones on a newly surfaced road that can fly up and damage vehicles.
Small stones on the road surface that can make tyres slip more easily.
Small loose stones on the road surface that can reduce tyre grip.
Large goods vehicles used to carry freight (UK term for trucks).
A large goods vehicle used for carrying cargo (also called a truck).
A large goods truck used to carry heavy loads (UK term for a truck).
A lower gear ratio that gives more engine control at slower speeds, often used on hills.
Planes flying near the ground, often near an airport approach.
Gears with more engine power and less speed, useful on hills.
High-beam headlights that light farther ahead but can dazzle other road users.
High-beam headlights that light farther ahead but can dazzle other road users.
Full high-beam headlights that light farther ahead but can dazzle other drivers.
A larger, busier road that smaller side roads join onto.
The high-intensity headlight setting (full beam) for dark roads with no oncoming traffic.
The more important road at a junction, which usually has priority.
An order you must follow, not just advice.
An order you must follow, not just advice.
A route you are required to follow, not just a suggested direction.
Rules you are legally required to obey.
A speed limit you must obey by law, often shown in a red circle or on overhead gantry signs.
A controlled driving movement such as reversing, turning, or parking.
The official owner’s manual from the car maker explaining controls and systems.
Small roadside posts that show distance markers and the direction to the nearest emergency phone.
